summary: Hebrew shows the direction of a movement with the same small prepositions it uses for place, put before the noun, which never changes: where to = לְ (לַשּׁוּק “to the market”, לְחֵיפָה “to Haifa”; formal אֶל), where from = מִ / מֵ (מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה “from work”), by what = בְּ (בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס “by bus”, בָּרַכֶּבֶת “by train”) and on foot = בָּרֶגֶל. Home(wards) is the single word הַבַּיְתָה (no לְ), and the questions are לְאָן? “where to?” and מֵאֵיפֹה? “where from?”. The verb carries the rest — and Hebrew, like German, splits “go”: הָלַךְ is going on foot (or going somewhere in town in general), נָסַע is going by any vehicle, as driver or passenger (gehen / fahren); the driver himself נוֹהֵג. Each verb has its preposition: נִכְנַס לְ… “go into”, יָצָא מִ… “go out of”, הִגִּיעַ לְ… “arrive at”, חִכָּה לְ… “wait for”, נִשְׁאַר בְּ… “stay at”, but עָזַב אֶת … “leave (behind)” takes a direct object. The verbs come from roots in different patterns (binyanim): pa‘al הָלַךְ / הוֹלֵךְ, nif‘al נִכְנַס / נִכְנָס, hif‘il הִגִּיעַ / מַגִּיעַ, pi‘el חִכָּה / מְחַכֶּה — the present tense still has just four forms, by gender and number. The direction itself is inside the verb (נִכְנַס “go in”, יָצָא “go out”, חָזַר “come back”), never in a particle added to it, and the way of moving is added only when it matters (בָּרֶגֶל “on foot”).

blocks.caption: The prefixes of lesson 11 again: בְּ and לְ swallow the article, מִ keeps it.

blocks.title: הַבַּיְתָה — home(wards), one word
blocks.text: Going home is הוֹלֵךְ הַבַּיְתָה, חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה — no לְ in front. Being at home is בַּבַּיִת. The final ־ָה is an old ending meaning “towards” (also in שְׂמֹאלָה “to the left”).

blocks.title: נָסַע, not הָלַךְ, for a bus, a car, a train
blocks.text: אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ לְחֵיפָה “I am going to Haifa (by bus / car / train)”. *אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לְחֵיפָה would mean you walk there. For a plane there is a verb of its own: טָס “fly”.

blocks.title: Into, out of, for
blocks.text: Entering takes לְ: נִכְנָס לַבַּיִת (German: in das Haus). Going out takes מִ: יוֹצֵא מֵהַבַּיִת. Waiting takes לְ: מְחַכֶּה לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס “waiting for the bus” — not בִּשְׁבִיל.

blocks.title: יָצָא or עָזַב?
blocks.text: יָצָא מִ… is going out of a place, often just for now: יוֹצֵא מֵהַבַּיִת בַּבֹּקֶר. עָזַב אֶת … is leaving behind — a city, a job, a person: עוֹזֵב אֶת הָעִיר.

blocks.title: Three prefixes, an unchanged noun
blocks.text: German needs a case for every direction (in die Stadt, in der Stadt, aus der Stadt); Hebrew uses three prefixes and leaves the noun alone: לָעִיר, בָּעִיר, מֵהָעִיר. “To” and “in” are always different words (לְ / בְּ), like German wohin / wo.

items.def: verb patterns (binyanim): the same root takes a different shape in each. הָלַךְ (pa‘al) · נִכְנַס, נִשְׁאַר (nif‘al, present without מ־: נִכְנָס) · חִכָּה (pi‘el, present מְחַכֶּה) · הִגִּיעַ (hif‘il, present מַגִּיעַ).

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is it on foot (הָלַךְ) or by vehicle (נָסַע)?
Towards (לְ, הַבַּיְתָה), out of (מִ), or staying (בְּ)?
Does the verb need its own preposition (נִכְנַס לְ, חִכָּה לְ, יָצָא מִ) or a direct object (עָזַב אֶת)?
Is there an article to fuse (לַ, בַּ) — or to keep (מֵהַ)?

askYourself: How does the person move? On foot → הָלַךְ (or רָץ); by bus, car, train → נָסַע; at the wheel → נָהַג; by plane → טָס.
Where to? → לְ + place (לַשּׁוּק, לְחֵיפָה); home → הַבַּיְתָה without לְ; formal → אֶל.
Where from? → מִ / מֵ + place (מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה, מֵחֵיפָה).
By what? → בְּ + vehicle (בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס, בָּרַכֶּבֶת); on foot → בָּרֶגֶל.
Which preposition does the verb itself take? נִכְנַס לְ, יָצָא מִ, הִגִּיעַ לְ, חִכָּה לְ, נִשְׁאַר בְּ — and עָזַב אֶת + object.
Who moves? → the present form by gender and number: הוֹלֵךְ / הוֹלֶכֶת / הוֹלְכִים / הוֹלְכוֹת.
steps: Choose the verb (on foot or by vehicle; in, out, back, arrive, stay, wait).
Put it in the present by the subject’s gender and number.
Add the direction with לְ / מִ / בְּ (or הַבַּיְתָה, בָּרֶגֶל), fusing the article with לְ and בְּ.

traps: *הוֹלֵךְ לְחֵיפָה for a trip by bus → נוֹסֵעַ לְחֵיפָה.
*נִכְנַס בַּבַּיִת → נִכְנַס לַבַּיִת (with בְּ it means “bumped into”).
*עוֹזֵב מֵהָעִיר → עוֹזֵב אֶת הָעִיר (or יוֹצֵא מֵהָעִיר).
The passenger does not נוֹהֵג: the driver נוֹהֵג, everybody נוֹסֵעַ.

quiz.q: “I am going to Haifa by bus” (a man speaking):
quiz.why: By vehicle the verb is נָסַע; הָלַךְ is on foot, and only the bus driver נוֹהֵג.
הַבַּיְתָה already means “to home”: no לְ. בַּבַּיִת is “at home”.
חִכָּה takes לְ: מְחַכֶּה לְ… “waits for …”.

quiz.q: “She leaves the city (she is moving away)”:
quiz.why: עָזַב takes a direct object with אֶת; יָצָא takes מִ (יוֹצֵאת מֵהָעִיר “goes out of the city”).
אֵיפֹה is “where (at)?”, מֵאֵיפֹה “where from?” — like wo / wohin / woher.
Entering takes לְ, and the present agrees with a woman: נִכְנֶסֶת.

seeAlso.note: Arabic uses إِلَى “to” (the same word as Hebrew אֶל), مِنْ “from” (= מִן / מִ) and بِـ “by” (بِالسَّيَّارَةِ “by car”), with the noun in the genitive; Hebrew nouns stay unchanged.
German splits “go” the same way: gehen (on foot) = הָלַךְ, fahren (by vehicle) = נָסַע; but German marks the direction with cases (in die Stadt / in der Stadt), Hebrew with לְ / בְּ.
Chinese uses 去 “go” / 来 “come”, 从 … 到 … “from … to …” and 坐 + vehicle (坐公共汽车 “take the bus”) before the verb.

notes.text: Greek σε covers both “to” and “in” (πάω στο σπίτι / είμαι στο σπίτι); Hebrew separates them: לַבַּיִת / בַּבַּיִת. And Greek πάω covers foot and vehicle, where Hebrew splits הָלַךְ / נָסַע.

Russian also splits идти / ехать (on foot / by vehicle) like הָלַךְ / נָסַע; but Russian builds direction with prefixes (войти, выйти, прийти), while Hebrew uses separate verbs: נִכְנַס, יָצָא, הִגִּיעַ.

Spanish also puts the direction in the verb (entrar, salir, volver ~ נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר) and adds the manner only if needed (a pie ~ בָּרֶגֶל). But ir covers foot and vehicle alike; Hebrew uses נָסַע for a vehicle.
English puts the direction in a particle (go in, go out, come back); Hebrew has a verb for each: נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר. “Go by bus” is נָסַע, never הָלַךְ.
As in French (entrer, sortir, revenir), the direction is in the verb: נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר. Aller covers both ways of going; Hebrew separates הָלַךְ (on foot) and נָסַע (by vehicle).

Like gehen / fahren, Hebrew splits הָלַךְ / נָסַע; but German puts the direction in particles (hineingehen, zurückkommen) and cases, Hebrew in the verb itself (נִכְנַס, חָזַר) and three prefixes (לְ / בְּ / מִ).

Hindi also has single verbs for “arrive” (पहुँचना), “return” (लौटना) and “go out” (निकलना), as Hebrew has הִגִּיעַ, חָזַר, יָצָא; but it marks the place with a postposition after it, Hebrew with a prefix before it.
Arabic, like Hebrew, has a verb for each direction (دَخَلَ, خَرَجَ, رَجَعَ, وَصَلَ ~ נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר, הִגִּיעַ) and the prepositions إِلَى / مِنْ ~ לְ / מִ.

Turkish adds a suffix for each direction (şehre, şehirde, şehirden); Hebrew uses three prefixes and leaves the noun alone: לָעִיר, בָּעִיר, מֵהָעִיר. Like Hebrew, Turkish puts the direction in the verb (girmek, çıkmak, dönmek).
Japanese also has verbs for each direction (入る, 出る, 帰る ~ נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר) but marks the place with a particle after it (家に, 家から); Hebrew uses a prefix before it.
Korean builds directions as compound verbs (들어가다 “go in”, 나가다 “go out”); Hebrew has one simple verb for each (נִכְנַס, יָצָא) and prefixes for the place.

Finnish shows where to / where / where from with cases (kaupunkiin, kaupungissa, kaupungista) and adds adverbs like sisään “in” and ulos “out”; Hebrew uses separate verbs (נִכְנַס, יָצָא) and three prefixes.
Hungarian puts the direction in verb prefixes (bemegy, kimegy, visszajön); Hebrew has a separate verb for each: נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר.
Swahili has a verb for each direction (kuingia “enter”, kutoka “go out”, kurudi “return”), as Hebrew does (נִכְנַס, יָצָא, חָזַר).
Chinese adds direction complements to the verb (走进去, 跑出来); Hebrew uses one verb that contains the direction (נִכְנַס, יָצָא) and adds the manner only if needed (בָּרֶגֶל).
Vietnamese strings verbs together (đi vào, chạy ra); Hebrew uses one verb with the direction in it: נִכְנַס, יָצָא.
Inuktitut marks the goal and the source with case endings (-mut “to”, -mit “from”) and builds the movement into one long verb; Hebrew uses separate words: a verb plus לְ / מִ.
